relations.note: Ọ̀rànmíyàn is Ajaka’s father in the principal Oyo royal genealogy.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 147–148

relations.note: Returning secretly, Oranmiyan withdraws rather than disturb his son’s successful reign.
Ọ̀rànmíyàn leaves Ajaka as regent; Ajaka is installed during his prolonged absence.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 147–148

relations.note: Johnson cautiously calls Moremi probably his wife; later Ifẹ̀ tradition makes the marriage definite.

god_relations.note: Ṣàngó is Ajaka’s younger brother, or half-brother in some later accounts.
god_relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 148–154

god_relations.note: Ṣàngó replaces the deposed Ajaka; Ajaka returns after Ṣàngó’s death.
god_relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 148–154

god_relations.note: Bahian traditions variously describe Dadá Ajaká as Xangô’s elder brother or sister.
god_relations.source: Querino and Verger traditions summarized by Castillo

god_relations.note: One Bahian variant identifies Dadá Ajaká as Xangô’s mother.
Some Bahian traditions treat Dadá Ajaká as a quality or form of Xangô.
god_relations.source: Querino, Verger, and later Bahian fieldwork

god_relations.note: Ajaka descends dynastically from Oduduwa through Ọ̀rànmíyàn; the intervening generations vary.
god_relations.source: Johnson and later Yoruba royal genealogies

god_relations.note: Aganju is Ajaka’s son and successor in the principal Oyo genealogy.
god_relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 154–155

god_relations.note: Isola’s epilogue invokes divine judgment to moralize Ẹfúnṣetán’s death.
Later harmonized genealogy makes him Moremi's father-in-law through her marriage to his son Ọ̀rànmíyàn.
Beier makes Moremi's sacrifice reconcile Odùduwà's polity with the spirits of displaced landowners.
Johnson makes Oranmiyan Oduduwa’s grandson through Okanbi.
god_relations.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

god_relations.note: Other Yoruba traditions make Oranmiyan the direct son of Oduduwa.
Johnson’s mythological scheme makes Oranmiyan the child of Oduduwa and Olokun.
god_relations.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

god_relations.note: Oranmiyan receives iron objects, a cock, and earth from Oduduwa’s divided property.
Ogun is Oranmiyan’s co-father and the source of his martial nature.
Olojo ritual associates their martial and iron-linked identities without equating them.
Johnson names Olokun as Oranmiyan’s mother and Oduduwa’s wife.
god_relations.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

god_relations.note: Some later retellings connect Orunmila’s divination with Oranmiyan’s foundation of Oyo.
Festival performances symbolically oppose Obatala groups to Oduduwa and Oranmiyan groups.

Egbeji.note: Egbeji serves Ajaka and disappears into heaven by climbing a suspended cord.
Egbeji.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 152–154

Egúngún Gbajero.note: The masquerade cried a warning or ritually authorized punishment before her murder.

Elenre.note: Elenre serves Ajaka as one of his named magical specialists.
Elenre.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 152–154

Elenre.note: Ajaka orders Elenre’s execution; the resulting wonder-tale produces Odo Elenre.
Elenre.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 152–154

Elà Olúorogbo.note: He is Moremi's only son, named variously Elà, Olúorogbo, or both.
Moremi yields her son as the demanded sacrifice; Johnson says he dies and joins the gods.

Elà Olúorogbo.myth: Ela revives and ascends to heaven
Elà Olúorogbo.note: In Ogumefu's variant, her sacrificed son revives, climbs heavenward, and promises to return.

Esimirin.myth: Moremi's vow before infiltrating the raiders
Esimirin.note: The river power grants or enables Moremi's success after receiving her vow.

Esimirin.myth: Payment of the promised river offering
Esimirin.note: After rejecting animal substitutes, the river power receives Moremi's only son as her promised offering.

Ijaehin.note: Ijaehin appears within Ajaka’s execution narrative but has no isolated direct exchange with him.
Ijaehin.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 152–154

Lakange Anihunka.note: Lakange bears Oranmiyan after relations with Ogun and Oduduwa or Okanbi.

Moremi.note: Johnson tentatively identifies Moremi as Oranmiyan’s wife; later accounts make the marriage certain.
Moremi.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

Moremi.note: Later popular accounts present Moremi and Oranmiyan as a fixed royal couple.

Obalufon II.note: Blier reconstructs Moremi's captors and opponents as forces associated with Obalufon and the earlier population.
Modern reconstructions make Oranmiyan a military participant in Obalufon II’s displacement.

Okanbi.note: Johnson identifies Okanbi as Oranmiyan’s father and Oduduwa as his grandfather.
Okanbi.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

Okanbi.note: One variant makes Okanbi, alongside Ogun, a father of Oranmiyan.

Olurogbo.note: Later genealogy makes Olurogbo Oranmiyan’s son through Moremi.

Orangun Ajagunla.note: Later Oyo accounts identify Orangun Ajagunla as Oranmiyan’s elder brother.
Orangun Ajagunla comes to assist Oranmiyan’s new Oyo against Borgu or Bariba forces.

Sango.note: Oranmiyan fathers Sango with a Nupe or Tapa princess.
Sango.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas
